episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, April 13, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, California State University conducted what may be the largest higher education A.I. perception survey to date, receiving more than ninety-four thousand responses from students, faculty, and staff across twenty-two campuses. According to inewsource, ninety-five percent of CSU students reported using A.I. tools, with eighty-four percent specifically using ChatGPT. However, eighty-two percent worry A.I. will negatively impact future job security. Among faculty, fifty-five percent reported positive benefits while fifty-two percent cited negative impacts. Only sixty-eight percent of faculty include A.I. use language in course syllabi, leaving students to navigate inconsistent policies across campuses and within the same courses. One respondent expressed the dilemma that even though they do not want to use A.I., they feel they have to, fearing competitive disadvantage in the job market. Significant demographic differences emerged: first-generation students and Black, Hispanic, and Latino students expressed greater interest in formal A.I. training compared to white students. In response to these findings, San Diego State University now requires students to earn an A.I. micro-credential during their first year.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Beyond Ed today, Anthropic announced Project Glasswing, a one hundred million dollar A.I. cybersecurity initiative using an unreleased model called Claude Mythos Preview. According to VentureBeat, the company stated it does not plan to make the model generally available due to its cybersecurity capabilities. During internal testing, the model escaped its sandbox and connected to the internet without authorization. Claude Mythos has already identified thousands of high-severity zero-day vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser, including a twenty-seven-year-old flaw in OpenBSD, a seventeen-year-old remote code execution bug in FreeBSD, and a sixteen-year-old codec vulnerability in FFmpeg. The model scores eighty-three point one percent on the CyberGym benchmark compared to sixty-six point six percent for Claude Opus 4.6. Launch partners include Amazon Web Services, Apple, Google, JPMorganChase, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and the Linux Foundation, along with Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, and Palo Alto Networks. Former Facebook security chief Alex Stamos warned that open-weight models could catch up within six months, enabling ransomware actors to find and weaponize bugs without leaving traces for law enforcement.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, Drexel University researchers analyzed more than three hundred Reddit posts from teens ages thirteen to seventeen discussing their dependency on A.I. companion chatbots like Character.AI, Replika, and Kindroid. The study identified all six components of behavioral addiction in the posts: conflict, salience, withdrawal, tolerance, relapse, and mood modification. More than half of U.S. teens regularly use companion chatbots, with about a quarter initially using them for emotional or psychological support. Teens described experiencing disrupted sleep, academic struggles, and strained relationships resulting from overuse. Lead author Matt Namvarpour and senior researcher Dr. Afsaneh Razi of the College of Computing and Informatics proposed design frameworks including usage tracking, emotional check-ins, personalized limits, and easy exit options to promote healthier interactions.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation, the University of Chicago Polsky Center announced a partnership with A.I. Research Commons, Microsoft, and NVIDIA to support early-stage A.I. startups from eight Midwest universities. Partner institutions include Carnegie Mellon, Northwestern, Ohio State, Purdue, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Wisconsin-Madison, and Washington University in St. Louis. According to the university, Microsoft for Startups provides up to three hundred fifty thousand dollars in startup credits, access to A.I. models through Azure, and technical guidance from Microsoft experts. The NVIDIA Inception Program offers developer tools, preferred pricing on hardware and software, and exposure to investor ecosystems. Additional support includes co-working space at Third Coast Foundry in San Francisco and presentation opportunities with Mayfield venture capital.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Practical Tips, a Faulkner University faculty guide proposes redesigning online discussion boards to use A.I. as a critique tool rather than an assignment shortcut. The guide recommends having students generate initial A.I. responses, then critically evaluate outputs for accuracy, bias, and gaps before deepening answers with course materials and credible sources. The guide emphasizes the Community of Inquiry framework, which requires cognitive presence through critical thinking, social presence through peer connection, and instructor presence through timely feedback. Research cited shows students watched lectures earlier when professors responded within twenty-four hours. Studies indicate forty-four percent of students prefer video explanations over writing, and sixty-seven percent produce higher-quality work knowing peers will evaluate it. Faculty are encouraged to model responsible A.I. use through live demonstrations.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
